item.title: Bird-Call Recognition Across Distance: Acoustic Degradation and BirdNET Performance
item.description: arXiv:2611.26757v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As bird calls weaken with distance, their recordings lose spectral detail. We examine how species recognition varies with distance using controlled playback of ten-second excerpts from 20 bird species at seven distances from 1 to 48 ft. An STM32-based recording system acquires and stores the audio, which is subsequently analyzed on a computer using acoustic measurements and BirdNET. Across four metadata configurations, mean-aggregated top-1 accuracy is 95--100% through 24 ft, 90--95% at 36 ft, and 80--90% at 48 ft, with 20 recordings evaluated per configuration at each distance. Across the screened recordings, the median upper spectral edge is below its 1-ft reference at every evaluated distance from 4 to 36 ft, indicating an overall reduction in upper-frequency content with distance. These results show that recognition remains high through 24 ft despite measurable spectral degradation, followed by greater and configuration-dependent losses at longer distances.
item.dc:creator: Hasmik Gharibyan, Bhaskar Krishnamachari

item.title: Efficient Conversational Multi-Talker ASR with Predicted Speaker-Agnostic Activity Streams
item.description: arXiv:2611.26796v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-talker automatic speech recognition (ASR) can be performed by conditioning a single-speaker recognizer on frame-level speaker activity. However, this approach requires a complete diarization pass to obtain the conditioning signals and one ASR pass per speaker, making both the frontend and recognition costs dependent on the number of speakers. We reduce these costs by using Heuristic Error Assignment Training (HEAT) to merge the activities of an arbitrary number of speakers into two speaker-agnostic streams. Conditioning on these streams limits recognition to two ASR passes regardless of the number of participants. Through an analysis of the resulting encoder representations, we show that under a stream-assignment heuristic suited to conversational speech, the recognizer represents a stream target much as it does a speaker target. Because the streams do not encode persistent speaker identities, we further replace the conventional sliding-window diarization and clustering frontend with a model that predicts both activity streams directly from the audio in a single pass. A combination of arrival-order and permutation-invariant training objectives over the two-stream powerset labels prevents the predictor from collapsing to identical streams. We also investigate post-hoc speaker attribution by matching decoded utterances to speaker activities within their assigned streams. Experiments on corpora with diverse conversational dynamics demonstrate a favorable efficiency--accuracy tradeoff. On AMI and ICSI, two-stream conditioning is respectively 44\% and 87\% faster than per-speaker conditioning using the same diarization frontend, with less than 2\% relative WER degradation. Direct activity prediction increases these speedups to 79\% and 132\%, with relative WER degradations of 10\% and 21\%, respectively.
item.dc:creator: Xiluo He, Magdalena Rybicka, Laureano Moro-Velazquez, Jes\'us Villalba, Thomas Thebaud, Najim Dehak

item.title: Emotion-Aware Prefix: Towards Explicit Emotion Control in Voice Conversion Models
item.description: arXiv:2603.09120v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent advances in zero-shot voice conversion have exhibited potential in emotion control, yet the performance is suboptimal or inconsistent due to their limited expressive capacity. We propose Emotion-Aware Prefix for explicit emotion control in a two-stage voice conversion backbone. We significantly improve emotion conversion performance, doubling the baseline Emotion Conversion Accuracy (ECA) from 42.40% to 85.50% while maintaining linguistic integrity and speech quality, without compromising speaker identity. Our ablation study suggests that a joint control of both sequence modulation and acoustic realization is essential to synthesize distinct emotions. Furthermore, comparative analysis verifies the generalizability of proposed method, while it provides insights on the role of acoustic decoupling in maintaining speaker identity.
item.dc:creator: Haoyuan Yang, Mu Yang, Jiamin Xie, Szu-Jui Chen, John H. L. Hansen

item.title: A Survey of Advancing Audio Super-Resolution and Bandwidth Extension from Discriminative to Generative Models
item.description: arXiv:2605.16681v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Audio super-resolution (SR), also referred to as bandwidth extension (BWE), aims to reconstruct high-fidelity signals from low-resolution (LR) or band-limited (BL) observations, an inherently ill-posed task due to the ambiguity of missing high-frequency (HF) content. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the field, with a particular focus on the paradigm shift from discriminative mapping to modern generative modeling. We first review early discriminative deep neural network (DNN) models, which formulate BWE/SR as a deterministic mapping problem and are prone to regression-to-the-mean effects and spectral over-smoothing. We then systematically review generative approaches, including autoregressive (AR) models, variational autoencoders (VAEs), generative adversarial networks (GANs), diffusion and score-based models, flow-based methods, and Schr\"odinger bridges. Across these approaches, we examine key design aspects, including representation domain, architecture, conditioning mechanisms, and trade-offs among reconstruction fidelity, perceptual quality, robustness, and computational efficiency. We further conduct unified experiments on representative discriminative and generative methods to provide controlled empirical evidence for these trade-offs. Furthermore, we discuss emerging directions involving large language models (LLMs) and multimodal foundation models, and highlight open challenges in perceptual evaluation, practical deployment, and real-world generalization. By providing a structured taxonomy and unified perspective, this survey establishes a comprehensive foundation and offers a practical roadmap for advancing BWE/SR from deterministic point estimation toward distribution-aware generative modeling.
item.dc:creator: Ningyuan Yang, Yize Li, Diego A. Cuji, Ryan M. Corey, Pu Zhao, Xue Lin, Andrew C. Singer

item.title: Asymmetric Phase Coding Audio Watermarking
item.description: arXiv:2605.07241v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The proliferation of deepfake audio challenges voice-based authentication, and passive forensic detectors are sensitive to evolving generative models and to real-world channel distortions. We propose Asymmetric Phase Coding (APC), a training-free cryptographic signing layer for audio that anyone holding the public key can verify offline, designed as a compact and auditable provenance primitive that can stand alone or be stacked with learned watermarks. APC combines Ed25519 digital signatures (EdDSA, FIPS 186-5; 64-byte signatures) with Reed-Solomon error correction, pseudo-random STFT phase-bin selection, and a redundant quantization-index-modulation (QIM) code on log-magnitude differences of adjacent bin pairs, yielding a compact, non-repudiable, blind-extractable watermark. A successful verification proves who signed the embedded message and that the message is intact. On 1,905 LibriSpeech test-clean clips (10 s, 44.1 kHz) under eight attack configurations (identity, 10% and 20% end-cropping, 8 kHz low-pass, 16 kHz round-trip resampling, FLAC, MP3 at 128 kbps and OGG-Vorbis at 128 kbps), APC verifies 98.3% to 99.8% of clips on every condition at an identity PESQ of 3.82 and accepts no wrong-key or unsigned clip. On 2,048 clips from 18 sets of 15 public corpora spanning music, meeting, telephone, multilingual and mostly vocoded speech, it verifies between 97.1% and 99.4%. It also survives platform processing chains, repeated MP3 and OGG coding at 128 kbps, cropping up to bounds predicted in closed form, integer time shifts through an optional decoder-side search, and the DNS64 and DeepFilterNet3 speech enhancers on most clips, and it verifies a signed 10 s clip in 3.17 ms on one CPU core. We compare APC with neural baselines (reproduced AudioSeal and WavMark, and published SilentCipher results), including a capacity-matched operating point, and show that it stacks with AudioSeal.
item.dc:creator: Guang Yang, Fengchen Liu, Amir Ghasemian, Zhong Wang, Ninareh Mehrabi, Homa Hosseinmardi
